record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.original_question: How can shear-induced memory effects and controlled shear histories in soft viscoelastic precursors—such as cement pastes, boehmite gels, cellulose-nanocrystal composites, structural-color precursors, dairy systems, yogurt, butter, and other foods—be used to tune microstructure, texture, porosity, optical properties, and final hardened-material performance?

evidence.quote: At fixed sample composition, it is, in principle, possible to build complex shear protocols to control precisely the texture of soft precursors and potentially inherit that texture in the hardened state of the material.
These examples illustrate the relevance of studying dairy products as model systems 271 to elucidate some of the open questions highlighted in the framework of this workshop.
6. Materials design – Use shear-induced memory effects to modify the properties of soft viscoelastic precursors employed to make hard materials, such as foodstuffs or cementitious materials.

artifact.category_tag: shear-induced memory in soft amorphous materials
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a soft viscoelastic precursor material (for example, a cement paste, a colloidal boehmite gel, a cellulose-nanocrystal composite suspension, a structural-color precursor colloidal dispersion, or a dairy-based system such as yogurt or butter) that undergoes a transition from a flowable state to a hardened or set state. Suppose that during the flowable stage the material can be subjected to a prescribed shear-history protocol γ(t) for t ∈ [0, T], producing measurable shear-induced memory effects (e.g., persistent anisotropy, residual stresses, structural reorganizations, or preferred microstructural orientations) that survive after cessation of flow and through the hardening process.

Develop a quantitative framework — comprising constitutive modeling of the precursor's viscoelastic/yield-stress response, descriptors of microstructural state (anisotropy tensors, pair-correlation functions, particle/aggregate orientation distributions, porosity fields), and mappings from the precursor's final microstructural state to the macroscopic properties of the hardened material (mechanical strength, texture, porosity, optical reflectance/transmittance, rheological signatures) — that answers the following:

(i) Given a target microstructure or set of target macroscopic properties of the hardened material (texture, porosity distribution, optical response, mechanical performance), determine whether there exists an admissible shear protocol γ(t) applied to the precursor such that the resulting hardened state realizes those target properties, and characterize the set of achievable targets as a function of composition.

(ii) Construct an explicit inverse-design procedure that, from the desired target, produces such a protocol γ(t), and quantify the sensitivity (stability) of the achieved hardened-state properties to perturbations of the protocol and of the precursor composition.

(iii) Identify the universal versus material-specific features of the precursor-to-product mapping across the listed classes of materials, and determine to what extent shear-induced memory in the precursor can be exploited to systematically tune final-state texture, porosity, optical, and mechanical properties.
artifact.status_search_result: This is posed as an open materials-design research direction concerning how shear-induced memory and controlled shear histories in soft viscoelastic precursors can be exploited to tune hardened-state microstructure and properties. Recent literature on shear memory in colloidal gels, structural-color materials, and cementitious pastes treats individual instances but no general predictive/inverse-design framework spanning these systems has been established; the problem appears to remain an open research program.

status_evidence.title: Shear-induced memory effects in boehmite gels
status_evidence.snippet: Memory effects in colloidal gels studied via controlled shear histories.
status_evidence.claim: Shear memory in soft gels is an active but unresolved research topic with system-specific findings.

status_evidence.title: Memory formation in matter (review)
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews memory effects in disordered and driven systems, identifying open questions in exploiting memory for materials design.
status_evidence.claim: General frameworks linking shear memory to hardened-material design remain open.
